title: Adaptive prefetch + per-prompt token clipping: onboarding eval notes
content:
Purpose and quick summary:

We ran a focused set of onboarding experiments for model v2.1 (decoder-only 7B-ish baseline) exploring two relatively under-explored levers for production cost/latency tradeoffs: an adaptive prefix prefetch (small KV cache prefill based on prompt signature + recent response tokens) and per-prompt dynamic max_token clipping. The goal was to find simple runtime knobs that give significant tail-latency and cost wins for our typical product prompt mix while keeping degradations in ROUGE/EM/QA F1 small and detectable.

Why this matters: batching and large static caches are good, but for many product prompts (short question -> short answer) we pay for long max_tokens and large caches we rarely use. If we can cheaply prefetch a small set of KV entries likely to be reused and truncate long generation budgets adaptively per prompt, we can reduce p95/p99 without large impact to quality and cost.

Experiment design (high level):
- Model: onboarding candidate v2.1 (7.1B trimmed weights, FP16, default sampling temperature 0.2)
- Workload: 3 promptsets derived from production telemetry: 
  * QA-short: 45k prompts, median input tokens 22, expected answer 8-40 tokens.
  * Assist-long: 15k prompts, median input tokens 110, expected answer 80-300 tokens.
  * Mixed-chat: 30k prompts, variable history length 0-6 turns, median expected output 64 tokens.
- Host infra: Dedicated test pool (A100s), same placement across runs to avoid droop.
- Metrics collected: p50/p95/p99 latency (ms), per-response token cost ($ per 1k tokens normalized), BLEU/ROUGE-L (where applicable), simple reg-test mixing metric: mean answer length diff and QA-F1 on labeled subset (1.2k QA examples). Also recording cache hit ratio, prefetch hit ratio, batch sizes seen.

Variants tested:
- Baseline: static batching (auto) + KV cache size 2MB per model instance (default), no prefetch, standard max_tokens 512.
- Prefetch-Small: same as baseline + adaptive prefix prefetch: for each prompt signature prefill last 32 KV entries if signature seen in last 5 minutes across instance pool.
- Prefetch-Large: prefill 128 KV entries under same policy.
- Clip-PerPrompt: baseline + per-prompt max_token clipping heuristic: target_max = min( max( 1.5*median_output_for_prompt_type, 32 ), 256 ).
- Prefetch+Clip: Prefetch-Small + Clip-PerPrompt.
- Aggressive-Clip: clip upper bound lowered to 128 for low-variance prompts.

Raw (aggregated) results (median across 3 runs, numbers approximate):

QA-short workload:
- Baseline: p50 62ms, p95 210ms, p99 410ms, cost normalized 1.00, QA-F1 87.4, avg_out_len 28
- Prefetch-Small: p50 58ms, p95 180ms, p99 330ms, cost 0.97, QA-F1 87.1, avg_out_len 28
- Prefetch-Large: p50 59ms, p95 175ms, p99 310ms, cost 0.99, QA-F1 87.0, avg_out_len 28
- Clip-PerPrompt: p50 60ms, p95 170ms, p99 300ms, cost 0.88, QA-F1 86.8, avg_out_len 24
- Prefetch+Clip: p50 55ms, p95 150ms, p99 260ms, cost 0.85, QA-F1 86.6, avg_out_len 24
- Aggressive-Clip: p50 54ms, p95 140ms, p99 240ms, cost 0.79, QA-F1 85.2, avg_out_len 20

Assist-long workload:
- Baseline: p50 180ms, p95 560ms, p99 1,200ms, cost 1.00, ROUGE-L 44.5, avg_out_len 160
- Prefetch-Small: p50 175ms, p95 540ms, p99 1,050ms, cost 0.98, ROUGE-L 44.4, avg_out_len 160
- Clip-PerPrompt: p50 178ms, p95 530ms, p99 1,020ms, cost 0.92, ROUGE-L 44.2, avg_out_len 142
- Prefetch+Clip: p50 170ms, p95 480ms, p99 900ms, cost 0.86, ROUGE-L 44.1, avg_out_len 140

Mixed-chat workload (higher variance):
- Baseline: p50 120ms, p95 680ms, p99 1,900ms, cost 1.00, mixed-quality delta baseline 0.0
- Prefetch-Small: p50 118ms, p95 620ms, p99 1,300ms, cost 0.98, quality -0.3
- Clip-PerPrompt: p50 115ms, p95 590ms, p99 1,100ms, cost 0.91, quality -0.7
- Prefetch+Clip: p50 108ms, p95 520ms, p99 900ms, cost 0.84, quality -1.2

Observations / interpretation:
1) Prefetching reduces tail latency especially for mixed-chat where short repeated prefixes occur (multi-turn). Small prefetch (32 entries) gives ~10-25% p95 reduction with negligible cost change; larger prefetch had diminishing returns and slightly higher memory overhead.
2) Per-prompt clipping delivers the strongest cost reductions (up to ~15-20% on average cost for long-answer workloads) and reduces p99 substantially by capping worst-case token budgets.
3) Combining both gives additive benefits: prefetch reduces the compute overhead of first-token/T0 paths while clipping reduces token-generation time and cost. For QA-short the combo achieved ~35% p99 reduction vs baseline.
4) Quality impacts are present but small for conservative clipping (upper bound 256). Aggressive clipping (upper bound 128) starts to show meaningful QA-F1 and ROUGE drops on complex prompts.
5) Regression detection: simple aggregate metrics (avg ROUGE, QA-F1) masked distributional failures. We found a small but real failure mode where long explanatory answers (rare 2% of QA-short) got truncated under Clip-PerPrompt leading to 0.6 absolute F1 hit for those queries. We need per-prompt signal or a fallback when clip triggers and model is predicted to need more budget.

Implementation notes and heuristics to carry forward:
- Use Prefetch-Small by default for onboarding candidate pools: low memory, cheap p95 wins. Policy: prefetch only if prompt signature seen >= 2 times in last 10 minutes and prefetched set size <= 32. Prefetch metadata stored with soft TTL 10 min.
- Implement Clip-PerPrompt conservative heuristic as opt-in: baseline clip target = min( max( 1.5*median_output_estimate, 32 ), 256 ). median_output_estimate derived from the prompt family mapping table (see linked confluence).
- Add a runtime safety: if clip triggers and the model emits an end-of-sequence token earlier than expected, log a high-priority alert for human review (this captures silent quality regressions).
- For mixed-chat / high-variance prompt families, do not clip aggressively; instead route them to instances with higher max_tokens budget or enable ephemeral burst capacity.

Regression detection and monitoring additions recommended:
- Add prompt-family-level baselines in the eval pipeline (median latency, median output length, QA-F1). Trigger alerts on >2% absolute drop in QA-F1 or >10% relative drop in ROUGE-L for any family with >=500 eval samples.
- Track clipped-rate per family. If clipped-rate > 3% and average answer length near clip bound, mark for immediate review.
- Correlate clip events with user-level retention/engagement samples (downstream signal) for production rollout.

Open questions and next steps:
- Can we get a cheap classifier to predict when a prompt will need >256 tokens? If >95% accurate, we can keep aggressive clipping for the rest. Explore small L0 classifier trained on prompt tokens + metadata (time of day, user tier).
- Evaluate cost/benefit on smaller models (3B) and larger models (13B) — clipping dynamics differ by model latency slope per token.
- Try hybrid prefetch: prefetch only top-k KV slots ranked by recency+importance (rather than contiguous 32/128) to reduce wasted prefetch.
- UX consideration: for customer-facing endpoints, expose a per-request "budget_hint" allowing clients to opt into higher max_tokens for specific requests.

Notes to reviewers:
- All raw traces and run configs are in linked GitHub PR + S3 bucket referenced in the Confluence page.
- This doc is intentionally conversational: it's a working capture of what we tried and what I'd recommend for the onboarding rollout for v2.1 candidates.
- If we push Prefetch+Clip to staged dedicated pools, we should gate by a small percent and run canary evals with labeled QA subsets.

Appendix (quick config snippets):
- Prefetch policy (pseudo): 
  if signature_count_last_10m >= 2 and instance_mem_free > 0.1: prefetch_kvs(signature, choose_top=32, ttl=600s)

- Clip heuristic (pseudo): 
  median_est = family_median_output(prompt_family)
  clip_bound = min(max(ceil(1.5 * median_est), 32), 256)
  if family_variance(prompt_family) > high_var_thresh: clip_bound = max(clip_bound, 256)

Raw experiment IDs: ONB-PF-2024-42 (prefetch sweep), ONB-CL-2024-57 (clip heuristics).

-- Aisha
